title: A diagnostic item measures one thing
statement: An item used to diagnose must test one piece of knowledge, because a wrong answer to a bundled item can't say what is missing.
example: With about 10 students per course, a bundled item can't be untangled by statistics, so it has to measure one thing by design.
detail: A diagnostic-assessment BrainLift worked through on AP courses names items that confound core knowledge with experience of the question format as a common failure, since a wrong answer then can't say why it is wrong (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback3/WF - Assessment  Feedback Brain - 260624-200115.md`, lines 310 and 336). With about 10 students per course at a time, a bundled item can't be decomposed statistically, so each item must measure one thing by design, in the simplest format that gives the information, and a multi-part item whose part (b) needs part (a) is split for diagnostics (lines 337, 397 and 402). It judges a diagnostic by whether students who follow its recommendations learn more efficiently (line 307), and the reading courses' adversarial review asks of every item whether a wrong answer identifies one component (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/course-red-team/references/finding-taxonomy.md`, line 165). Test that knowledge in the plainest format that shows it, and split dependent parts into separate items; bundled items are often exam-style ones.
against: Both sources allow a stimulus-based item when the stimulus is the skill, as in reading comprehension (the BrainLift, line 397; the checklist, line 165), and the reading comprehension BrainLift holds that no valid diagnostic comprehension test exists (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/teaching-reading-comprehension-brainlift.md`, lines 88-89). The taxonomy makes one exception for reading: bundling is acceptable when the stimulus itself is the knowledge component being tested, with everything else stripped (`ti-courseplans-audit/skills/course-red-team/references/finding-taxonomy.md`).
